The Flood We Refuse to Name: Corruption, Collusion, and the Crisis Beneath Our Streets
By Dr. Tony Leachon

In the Philippines, floods are no longer seasonal—they are systemic. They arrive not only with rain, but with resignation. Streets turn into rivers, classrooms into shelters, and homes into islands. 

Yet behind every submerged barangay lies a deeper truth: the deluge is not just water. It is waste. Waste of public funds, waste of planning, and waste of moral leadership.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. recently disclosed that 20% of the ₱545 billion flood control budget was awarded to just 15 contractors. That revelation should have triggered a national reckoning. Instead, it was met with a shrug. 

We have normalized the abnormal. We have accepted that our children will wade through contaminated waters while a handful of firms—shielded by anonymity and political protection—profit from our pain.

This is not merely a failure of infrastructure. It is a failure of integrity.

Flood control, by its very nature, demands foresight, transparency, and science. It requires hydrological modeling, urban planning, and community engagement. Yet what we see instead is a pattern of collusion: recycled contractors, opaque bidding processes, and projects that begin with ribbon-cuttings but end in ruin. The water recedes, but the corruption remains.

The consequences are not abstract. They are lived. Leptospirosis cases surge. Traffic paralyzes cities. Schoolchildren miss days of learning. Families lose livelihoods. And amid it all, the public grows weary—not just of the floods, but of the futility of protest.

We must break this cycle.

First, we must demand full disclosure. The Securities and Exchange Commission holds the key to identifying the true owners of these favored firms. Let us retrieve those records and expose the networks behind the contracts. Let sunlight be our disinfectant.

Second, we must empower independent oversight. The Commission on Audit and the Senate Blue Ribbon Committee must act not as spectators but as sentinels. Their mandate is not to protect reputations but to protect the Republic.

Third, we must elevate the right voices. Leaders like Senator Panfilo Lacson, Mayor Benjamin Magalong, Mayor Vico Sotto, and Mayor Joy Belmonte—who has long navigated the complexities of Quezon City’s urban challenges—must be empowered to lead with integrity and courage. Their example reminds us that governance can still be principled, even in the most difficult terrain.

Fourth, we must educate the public. Civic literacy is our first line of defense. Let us teach our youth that governance is not a spectator sport. That transparency is not optional. That public service is not a business venture.

And finally, we must restore dignity to disaster response. Floods will come again. Climate change ensures that. But if we do not reform our systems now, we will face not just rising waters—but rising cynicism.

I write this not only as a physician and advocate, but as a father and grandfather. I think of my granddaughters, Lily Bear and Simmy, and the world they will inherit. I think of the quiet rituals we share—museum strolls, gentle songs, simple meals. I want them to grow up in a country where public service is sacred, not sold. Where resilience is built not just on concrete, but on conscience.

The flood is not just outside our homes. It is inside our institutions. And it is time we named it.

Let this be our moment of clarity. Let this be our turning point.

#RelentlessForChange 
#KleptopirosisIsReal 
#HopeInService 
#HealthWithHonor
